faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Punta Gorda?
faqs.a: Punta Gorda quotes split between historic and canal construction. Historic homes cost more in labor because exclusion must preserve original materials; canal homes cost more when seawall and dock entries join the roof work. We inspect the full property, price each element openly, and give the total in writing before starting.

faqs.q: A tortoise burrow appeared on my Punta Gorda lot — what are my options?
faqs.a: A gopher tortoise burrow is protected ground. The tortoise is State Threatened, and you may not move, harm, or disturb the animal, its burrow, or its eggs without an FWC permit; construction within 25 feet of the burrow needs that permit, and relocation is done only by an FWC Authorized Gopher Tortoise Agent to a permitted recipient site. Our role is identification and honest direction — confirming the burrow is a tortoise's rather than an armadillo's, marking the buffer, and pointing you to the FWC tortoise program. Do not let anyone sell you a same-week tortoise removal.

Punta Gorda.wildlife_intro:
Punta Gorda's canal finger neighborhoods in Punta Gorda Isles and Burnt Store Isles put nearly every home on the water, and the historic district's early-1900s houses add a second, older layer of work. Seawall raccoons, roof rats in the palms along Marion Avenue, and iguanas — established here in Charlotte County's southern warmth — share the call sheet with a uniquely local regular: gopher tortoises on the undeveloped lots scattered through the canal grids, whose burrows stop more than one pool project for a permitting talk.

Historic-district houses need a gentler hand: original wood siding and aging rooflines cannot take aggressive sealing, so we match exclusion to the structure. For canal homes the inspection includes the seawall and dock. Burrowing animals get identified before anything is trapped — a tortoise burrow with its half-moon apron means referral and a 25-foot buffer; an armadillo's scattered cone-shaped holes mean a removal plan we can start the same week.

faqs.q: Why do animals keep coming back to my Port Charlotte home?
faqs.a: Usually because the cover next door never left. Port Charlotte's vacant lots hold raccoons, opossums, and tortoises year-round, and an unsealed or partly sealed house is simply the best den on the block. Lasting control here means a complete exclusion — every soffit corner, vent, and roof return screened or flashed — plus removing invitations like pet food on the lanai and fallen fruit. We will show you the entries we found and which ones matter most if budget forces a sequence.

Port Charlotte.wildlife_intro:
Port Charlotte is a vast platted grid — thousands of Gulf-access and freshwater canal lots, many still vacant and wooded, stitched between the built streets. Vacant-lot cover is the story here: raccoons and opossums commute from undeveloped lots into adjacent attics, armadillos dig the sandy yards, eastern moles ridge the lawns, and gopher tortoises hold burrows on the empty parcels. Roof rats thrive in the canal palms, and the Murdock commercial corridor's older low buildings add pigeon and bat work.

Because the lot next door is often the habitat, Port Charlotte exclusions have to be thorough — sealing one hole while the soffit line stays soft just moves the animal ten feet. We harden the entire roofline, and for homes beside vacant land we talk frankly about recurrence pressure and what trimming and lot-edge habits reduce it. Traps are checked daily, and natives are released under the same-county, 40-acre, written-permission rule or on your own lot.

faqs.q: Sandhill cranes are damaging my Rotonda West screens — what can I do?
faqs.a: Less than you'd hope, and anyone promising removal is misleading you. Florida sandhill cranes are State Threatened and protected; the lawful tools are deterrence — motion-activated sprayers, keeping pet food and seed off the lanai, and never feeding them, which Florida rule prohibits. Cranes peck at reflective glass and screens most during breeding season and usually move on. We will confirm the birds and the damage pattern and outline deterrent options, but the cranes themselves are an FWC matter, not a trapping job.

Rotonda West.wildlife_intro:
Rotonda West is unmistakable from the air — a circular community of wedge-shaped lots around canals and golf fairways, wedged between preserves on the Cape Haze peninsula. The geometry delivers wildlife to every door: raccoons travel the canal banks, sandhill cranes stalk the fairways and occasionally peck at screens, gopher tortoises burrow on the undeveloped wedges, and bobcats pass through at dawn — a look-and-appreciate animal, not a service call. Attic work is the familiar Gulf Coast set: roof rats, gray squirrels, and the odd opossum in a garage.

Rotonda's many seasonally empty homes deserve a specific mention: a house that sits quiet for months is exactly what a roof rat colony wants, and we often find the damage when owners return. We offer pre-departure sealing checks for seasonal residents and prioritize full exclusion over trap-only visits for homes that will sit empty. Cranes and tortoises on your lot are explained and referred, never handled — feeding a sandhill crane is actually illegal in Florida, a fact many new residents are surprised by.

faqs.q: An alligator is hanging around our Charlotte Harbor dock — can you remove it?
faqs.a: No, and be wary of anyone who says yes. Nuisance alligators in Florida are handled only through FWC's Statewide Nuisance Alligator Program, which sends its own contracted trappers; an alligator of four feet or more that threatens people, pets, or property qualifies for that program. Keep people and pets back from the water's edge, never feed it — feeding wild alligators is illegal and trains them to approach — and make the report to FWC. Our crew handles the raccoon in your attic; gators belong to the state program.

Charlotte Harbor.wildlife_intro:
Charlotte Harbor the community — the unincorporated waterfront across the bridges from Punta Gorda — is older, shadier, and more working-waterfront than its canal-planned neighbors. Big oaks shade 1950s and 60s houses along Bayshore Drive, the harbor itself is a few steps from most doors, and the mangrove fringe shelters raccoons that den in those old roofs. Roof rats run the oak canopy, armadillos work the shell-and-sand yards, and mullet schools and wading birds keep the shoreline busy behind the homes.

Older construction defines our Charlotte Harbor work: brittle shingles, patched soffits, and additions joined at odd angles create entry mazes that need patient mapping. We photograph every opening so you see the plan before paying for it. Bats in these older rooflines are handled seasonally — exclusion between August 15 and April 15 only — and any alligator that takes up residence in a harbor-side ditch is referred to FWC's nuisance alligator program, which uses its own contracted trappers; that is never a private booking.

faqs.q: How can I tell an armadillo burrow from a tortoise burrow in Harbour Heights?
faqs.a: Look at the shape and the doorstep. A gopher tortoise burrow is a half-moon — flat floor, curved roof — with a wide fan of excavated sand (the apron) out front, often in open sunny ground. An armadillo burrow is rounder, smaller, and tucked against a slab, log, or stump, with scattered cone-shaped feeding holes across the nearby lawn. If it is a tortoise, the answer is a 25-foot no-work buffer and an FWC referral; if it is an armadillo, we can trap it, and a live-trapped armadillo may be released on your land or within Charlotte County on 40-plus acres with written permission.

Harbour Heights.wildlife_intro:
Harbour Heights is a small, quiet river community east of Punta Gorda where the Peace River bends through oak hammock and most streets end at the water or the woods. Lots are larger, outbuildings common, and the wildlife pressure is rural in character: raccoons in attics and boat sheds, armadillos and moles working big sandy yards, opossums in crawl spaces, and the occasional pygmy rattlesnake in palmetto at a lot's wild edge. Gopher tortoises are part of the neighborhood fabric here.

Small-community work runs on identification first. We confirm whether the burrow by your shed is a tortoise's — protected, buffered, referred — or an armadillo's, which we can trap. River-edge homes also get a cottonmouth conversation: the species lives along the Peace River banks, and we would rather walk your dock area and point out habitat than sell fear. Call (844) 544-3498 — for a community this size, one thorough visit usually settles the whole property.
